Date: 2022-06-16
REMARKS
In view of the claim amendments below remarks, the Examiner is respectfully requested to reconsider the rejections.
Office Action Summary
Claims 22 and 33 were objected to because of informalities. Claims 22-24, 33 and 34 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, for insufficient antecedent basis. Claim(s) 16-20, 26-31, and 35 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 (a)(1) as being anticipated by Gillian et al., (US20170097413A1) (hereinafter "Gillian"). Claims 21, 22, 32, and 33 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 20 and 31 above, and further in view of Hauenstein et al., (US20170095181A1), (hereinafter "Hauenstein"). Claim 23 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 18 above, and further in view of Sun et al., (US20120203491A1) (hereinafter "Sun") and Komaromi et al., (US20160162256A1) (hereinafter "Komaromi"). Claims 24 and 34 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 20 above, and further in view Rogers, (US20170351827A1) (hereinafter "Rogers"). Claim 25 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Gillian as applied to claim 20 above, and further in view Kim et al., "Tracking a Moving Target with Multiple Doppler Sensors Using an Artificial Neural Network", IEEE Antennas and Propagation Society International Symposium, June 9-15, pp. 1477-1480, (hereinafter "Kim").
Claim Objections
Claims 22 and 33 have been amended to remove the comma between "native sensor data" and "when the sensor".
35 U.S.C. § 112
Claims 22 and 23 have been amended to recite "a user equipment" for antecedent basis. Claim 33 recites "the user equipment" as "user equipment" has been amended into claim 27. Claims 24 and 34 has been amended to recite alternative subject matter.
35 U.S.C. § 1021103
The Examiner is respectfully requested to withdraw the rejections based on Sections 102 and 103, because the prior art does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of the independent claims. MPEP 2131 ("A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference."); MPEP 2143.03 ("All words in a claim must be considered in judging the patentability of that claim against the prior art.").
1. Independent claims 27, 35, Dependent claim 23: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user, the sensor data indicative of the activity of the user
Independent claim 27 has been amended to claim:
"wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user, the sensor data indicative of the activity of the user."
Independent claim 35 has been amended similarly, and dependent claim 23 recites a similar feature.
Support for this amendment is found within Applicant's filed specification at page 8, lines 16-17, page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2, FIG. 3B, and original claim 23.
Gillian FIG. 6 describes "provide radar field" (602), "receive one or more reflection signals" (604), "transform the one or more reflection signals to provide radar data" (606), "extract, from the radar data, a radar feature indicating a target characteristic" (608).
Gillian paragraph [0092 describes "At 606, the one or more reflection signals are transformed into radar data representations. The reflection signals may be transformed using any suitable signal processing, such as by performing a range-Doppler transform, range profile transform, micro-Doppler transform, IIQ transform, or spectrogram transform. Continuing the ongoing example, the radar sensor performs a range-Doppler transform to provide target velocity and direction information for the user's hand." Sun paragraph [0035] describes "Thus, under this context (e.g., high physical activity), the system 100 stops collecting and/or processing data at the physiological sensor or sensors while the user is active. Using the context information collected at the first sensor or group of sensors (e.g., the accelerometer data) to stop data collection and/or processing at the second sensor or group of sensors enables the system 100 to: (1) save resources (e.g., battery life of the sensor), and (2) increase the accuracy of the sensor data analysis by avoiding collecting data when artifacts can reduce the quality of the data."
Komaromi paragraph [0015] describes "The action triggered is subject to the kind of wearable electronic device. However, for any wearable electronic device, one action may be to either power down or to switch to a stand-by mode if the output signal changes from a detected "on-body" state-i.e. the device is worn by a user-to an "off-body" state-i.e. the device is detected to no longer be worn."
Komaromi paragraph [0036] describes "One or more of powering the sensor/s, evaluating, or logging of data from the further sensor/s preferably is stopped or paused in response to the device no longer being detected to be worn."
The Examiner stated on pages 10-11 of the Office Action, regarding claim 23 which subject matter has now been incorporated into independent claims 27 and 35, that Gillian describes the pseudo sensor data feature of independent claims 27 and 35, but does not disclose data derived in response to an indication due to context information:
Regarding claim 23, Gillian teaches the method of claim 18, further teaching the pseudo sensor data.
However Gillian fails to explicitly disclose data derived in response to an indication due to context information.
The Examiner stated on page 11 of the Office Action, regarding claim 23, that Sun at the above-referenced excerpt ([0035]) teaches data derived in response to an indication due to context information:
In the same activity level tracking field of endeavor, Sun teaches data derived in response to an indication due to context information ([0035] the sensor uses context Information to decide whether or not to collect data).
The Examiner stated on page 11 of the Office Action, regarding claim 23, that Komaromi at the above-reference excerpts ([0015], [0036]) teaches an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is not providing native sensor data:
In the health or fitness device field of endeavor, Komaromi teaches an indication that the user equipment or the sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user ([0015] an action is triggered when the device detects if it is "on-body" or "off- body" [0036] the logging of data is stopped when the device is no longer worn, meaning the native sensor data is not being provided).
However, Gillian, Sun and Komaromi alone or in combination do not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user, the sensor data indicative of the activity of the user.
This is because Sun describes that the system stops collecting data in response to user activity, not deriving data in response to native sensor data not being provided. Refer to Sun paragraph [0035]: "under this context (e.g., high physical activity), the system 100 stops collecting and/or processing data at the physiological sensor or sensors while the user is active." Sun implements this action due to unreliability of the data during certain types of physical activity. Refer to Sun paragraph [0035]: "during vigorous physical activity, physiological sensor data can be unreliable." Thus Sun describes the opposite of Applicant's method, where in Applicant's method the pseudo sensor data is provided in response to native sensor data not being provided.
Similarly, Komaromi describes stopping or pausing logging of sensor data, such as in response to a device not being worn, not deriving data in response to native sensor data not being provided. Refer to Komaromi paragraph [0036]: "logging of data from the further sensor/s preferably is stopped or paused in response to the device no longer being detected to be worn." In Komaromi this is done to save power. Refer to Komaromi paragraph [0016]: "one action may be to either power down or to switch to a stand-by mode if the output signal changes from a detected "on-body" state-i.e. the device is worn by a user-to an "off-body" state-i.e. the device is detected to no longer be worn." Thus Komaromi describes the opposite of Applicant's method, where in Applicant's method the pseudo sensor data is provided in response to native sensor data not being provided.
Gillian also does not describe that the "radar feature indicating a target characteristic" (refer to Gillian Fig. 6 item 608") is derived in response to an indication of native sensor data not being available, or that the data provided from the sensor fusion engine 110 (refer to Gillian Fig. 5) is derived in response to an indication of native sensor data not being available.
In contrast, a main idea of Applicant's invention is to provide the pseudo sensor data from the RF based tracker 110 in response to the native sensor data not being available, for example when fitness tracker 104 comprising a native sensor is docked or not being worn by the user 102. The idea is to provide a continuous stream of sensor data so that there are no gaps in the data to be analyzed by the application of the fitness tracker 104.
Thus, the unavailability of the native sensor data triggers the deriving of the pseudo sensor data from the RF based tracker 110.
Refer e.g. to Applicant's filed specification at page 8, lines 16-17 ("the gap may be defined by a message or trigger signal indicating that the sensor 399 is not able to generate sensor data").
Refer also to Applicant's filed specification at page 11, line 38 to page 12, line 2 ("the health and fitness tracker 104 may trigger the RF based tracker 110 to track the user in response to the health and fitness tracker 104 transmitting an indication, such as by transmitting a trigger signal or sending a message, to the RF based tracker 110").
FIG. 3B of Applicant's filed disclosure illustrates this idea:
Indication received, so pseudo sensor data derived between time t1
SVG
{EMBED HERE}

FIG. 3B
As can be seen above, in Applicant's case, at time tt, the native sensor data is not available (e.g. because the fitness tracker 104 is charging). Upon receiving the indication that the native sensor data is not available at time ti, between time t1 and time t2 the pseudo sensor data is derived. At time t2, the native sensor data becomes available again, so the pseudo sensor data is no longer derived (refer also to amended claim 34). This aspect is not described by the combination of Gillian, Sun, and Komaromi.
Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user, the sensor data indicative of the activity of the user. Independent claim 27, on the other hand, claims (with a similar feature being in independent claim 35 and dependent claim 23) "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to an indication that a user equipment or a sensor is not providing native sensor data for the user, the sensor data indicative of the activity of the user". This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, independent claims 27 and 35, and dependent claim 23 are patentable and should be allowed.
2. Independent claim 16: the prior art does not disclose or suggest providing the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user
Independent claim 16 has been amended to claim:
"providing the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user."
Support for this amendment is found within Applicant's filed specification at page 4, lines 28-31, page 6, lines 21-22, page 7, lines 27-30, and original claim 20. The subject matter of original claim 20 has been amended into claim 16.
Gillian paragraph [0073] describes "As another example, consider a scenario in which the signal transformer 502 transforms the raw radar data into a measure of the target object's velocity over time. In turn, the feature abstractor 504 uses this information to identify a finger fast-tap motion by using a threshold value to compare the target object's velocity of acceleration to the threshold value, a slow-tap feature, and so forth. Any suitable type of algorithm can be used to extract a feature, such as machine-learning algorithms implemented by a machine-learning component (not shown) of the digital signal processor 126."
Gillian paragraph [0094] describes "At 610, a sensor is activated based on the radar feature. The sensor can be activated to provide supplemental data. In some cases, a sensor is selected for activation based on the radar feature or a type of the radar feature." Gillian paragraphs [0077]-[0078] describe "The user detection application 524 may detect, based on sensor data or radar data, presence of a user...In some embodiments, the activity detection application 526 uses the sensor data and the radar data to detect activity in the computing device 102's environment."
The Examiner stated on page 3 of the Office Action, regarding claim 16, that Gillian at the above-referenced paragraph ([0073]) describes the feature "the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least a machine learning model configured to transform the radio frequency based data into the pseudo sensor data", asserting that Gillian teaches extracting features such as target objects' velocities using a machine learning model.
The Examiner stated on page 4 of the Office Action, regarding claim 16, that Gillian at the above-referenced paragraph ([0094]) describes the feature "providing the pseudo sensor data", asserting that Gillian describes that the radar is providing data to a sensor.
The Examiner stated on pages 4-5 of the Office Action, regarding claim 20, that Gillian at the above-referenced paragraphs ([0077]-[0078]) describes the feature "wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and the native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user", asserting that that Gillian describes that the user detection application tracks the user in the environment as well as activity.
However, Gillian does not disclose or suggest providing the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user, for at least two reasons.
First, Gillian does not describe pseudo sensor data derived based on a machine learning model. Gillian at paragraph [0073] describes that "the signal transformer 502 transforms the raw radar data into a measure of the target object's velocity over time." However, the signal transformer 502 does not use machine learning to do the transformation. The machine learning model is only used in the feature extractor 504, which is used for identification, e.g. identification of a finger fast-tap motion or a slow-tap motion, and not for providing pseudo sensor data. Refer to Gillian paragraph [0073].
The Examiner is therefore combining the signal transformer 502 embodiment with the machine learning embodiment of the feature extractor 504 to arrive at anticipation under Section 102, which is not permitted under Microsoft Corp. v. Biscotti, Inc., 878 F.3d 1052, 1064-1067 (Fed. Cir. 2017) (Federal Circuit upholding PTAB's determination that multiple, distinct teachings of the prior art did not render the claims anticipated).
In contrast, Applicant uses machine learning to derive the pseudo data by transforming the RF based data. Applicant's idea is therefore to use machine learning within Gillian's signal transformer 502 (not done by Gillian). Refer to Applicant's filed specification at page 4, lines 28- 31: "the RF based tracker may include a machine learning (ML) model that is trained, or configured to, transform the RF based data indicative of the user's activity into pseudo sensor data, such pseudo accelerometer data and/or other types of sensor data, which may be representative of the user's activity." Gillian's signal transformer 502 does not use machine learning.
Second, Gillian does not describe providing the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user. Gillian at paragraph [0094] only describes that "a sensor is activated based on the radar feature", not providing pseudo sensor data based on radio frequency (RF) data, such as radar, to an application. Even though Gillian at paragraph [0094] describes "data may be received from a microphone or depth sensor to improve a detection feature", the detection feature uses native microphone or native depth sensor data, not pseudo sensor data based on the radar.
While Gillian at paragraph [0077] describes "The user detection application 524 may detect, based on sensor data or radar data, presence of a user", and Gillian at paragraph [0078] describes "the activity detection application 526 uses the sensor data and the radar data to detect activity in the computing device 102's environment" Gillian does not describe that the activity detection application 526 uses pseudo sensor data. For example, Gillian does not describe that the activity detection module 526 uses data from the signal transformer 502 or the feature extractor 504. The sensor data and the radar data used by the activity detection module 526 is the sensor data 506 and the radar data 508 fused by the sensor fusion engine 110, or the original sensor data 506 and the original radar data 508.
In contrast, Applicant describes at page 7, lines 27-30 that "the native sensor data in the form of, for example, accelerometer data 380A-B, 382A-B, and 384A-B along with the pseudo sensor data 390, 392, and 394 may be provided to an application 390", where the pseudo sensor data is a result of transformation of radio frequency (RF) based data using a machine learning model. Refer to Applicant's filed specification at page 4, lines 28-31: "the RF based tracker may include a machine learning (ML) model that is trained, or configured to, transform the RF based data indicative of the user's activity into pseudo sensor data, such pseudo accelerometer data and/or other types of sensor data, which may be representative of the user's activity." Gillian does not describe the activity detection application 526 using such pseudo sensor data derived from a machine learning model.
Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest providing the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user. Claim 16, on the other hand, claims "providing the pseudo sensor data derived based on at least the machine learning model to an application to enable the application to process the pseudo sensor data and native sensor data to enable tracking the activity of the user." This is not disclosed or suggested in the prior art. Therefore, claim 16 is patentable and should be allowed.
3. Dependent claim 26: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to at least one gap in the native sensor data, the at least one gap caused at least in part with a sensor, that generates the native sensor data representative of activity of the user, not being able to generate the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user
Dependent claim 26 has been amended to claim:
"wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to at least one gap in the native sensor data, the at least one gap caused at least in part with a sensor, that generates the native sensor data representative of activity of the user, not being able to generate the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user."
Support for the amendment to claim 26 is found within Applicant's filed specification at original claims 21 and 32, as well as page 8, lines 12-17, and FIG. 3B.
Regarding the rejection of claims 21 and 32, the Examiner does not apply a citation to reject the aspect "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to at least one gap in the native sensor data, the at least one gap caused at least in part by the sensor not being able to generate the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user." Refer to pages 8-10 of the Office Action.
It is believed that the Examiner does not apply a citation to this aspect of claims 21 and 32 because claims 21 and 32 recite "or", such that "wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to at least one gap in the native sensor data, the at least one gap caused at least in part by the sensor not being able to generate the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user" is an alternative.
It is respectfully submitted that the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is derived in response to at least one gap in the native sensor data, the at least one gap caused at least in pait with a sensor, that generates the native sensor data representative of activity of the user, not being able to generate the native sensor data representative of the activity of the user.
This is a main idea of Applicant's invention, the idea being to provide a continuous stream of sensor data so that there are no gaps in the data to be analyzed by the application of the fitness tracker 104. Thus, the unavailability of the native sensor data triggers the deriving of the pseudo sensor data from the RF based tracker 110 to fill the gap in the data, as shown by Applicant's FIG. 3B, where the pseudo sensor data 370 bridges the gap between native sensor data 360A and native sensor data 360B. Such a bridging of the gap in native sensor data is not disclosed or suggested by the prior art. Therefore, dependent claim 26 is patentable for this additional reason.
4. Dependent claim 20: the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided from a first device that generates to the pseudo sensor data to a second device comprising the application to process the pseudo sensor data and the native sensor data, the native sensor data generated with the second device using the sensor
Dependent claim 20 has been amended to claim:
"wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided from a first device that generates the pseudo sensor data using the machine learning model to a second device comprising the application to process the pseudo sensor data and the native sensor data, the native sensor data generated with the second device using the sensor."
Support for the amendment to claim 20 is found within Applicant's filed specification at FIG. 1 (health and fitness tracker device 104, RF based tracker device 110), FIG. 8, page 4, line 38 to page 5, line 1, and page 12, lines 14-16 ("For example, the RF-based tracker 110 (or other processor-based device) may provide the pseudo sensor data, via a wireless and/or wired interface, to the application 390 at a device, such as the health and fitness tracker 104 or other device.").
Gillian paragraph [00941 describes "At 610, a sensor is activated based on the radar feature."
The Examiner stated on page 4 of the Office Action that Gillian at the above-referenced paragraph ([0094]) describes the element "providing the pseudo sensor data" of claim 16:

However, Gillian does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided from a first device that generates the pseudo sensor data using the machine learning model to a second device comprising the application to process the pseudo sensor data and the native sensor data, the native sensor data generated with the second device using the sensor.
This is because Gillian only describes at paragraph [0094] that "a sensor is activated based on the radar feature." In Gillian all of the functionality is embedded within the same device, namely computing device 102. For example, in Gillian FIG. 1 the sensor-based applications 108, the sensor fusion engine 110, the sensors 118, and the radar sensor 120 are all within the same computing device 102, where with reference to Gillian FIG. 5, the sensor-based applications 108 include the activity detection application 526.
In contrast, in Applicant's use case, the RF based tracker 110 comprising the machine learning model 815 generates the pseudo sensor data which is provided to an application 390 of a different device, such as the health and fitness tracker device 104. Refer to Applicant's filed specification at page 12, lines 14-16 ("For example, the RF-based tracker 110 (or other processor- based device) may provide the pseudo sensor data, via a wireless and/or wired interface, to the application 390 at a device, such as the health and fitness tracker 104 or other device.").
The use case described by Applicant at page 6, lines 16-24 of Applicant's filed specification is that "The user 102 may, as noted, remove the health and fitness tracker 104 (and/or remove the sensor). When this is the case, the RF based tracker 110 (which may include one or more radios such as one or more UWB radars, for example) may track the user's 102 activity. For example, the user may be in a room, and as the user walks around the room, the RF based tracker may receive RF signal returns from the user. The received RF signals may be decoded and/or digitized into RF based data." The prior art including Gillian does not disclose or suggest this use case,
Accordingly, the prior art does not disclose or suggest wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided from a first device that generates the pseudo sensor data using the machine learning model to a second device comprising the application to process the pseudo sensor data and the native sensor data, the native sensor data generated with the second device using the sensor. Dependent claim 20, on the other hand, claims "wherein the pseudo sensor data is provided from a first device that generates the pseudo sensor data using the machine learning model to a second device comprising the application to process the pseudo sensor data and the native sensor data, the native sensor data generated with the second device using the sensor." This is not disclosed or suggested by the prior art. Therefore, dependent claim 20 is patentable for this additional reason and should be allowed.
5. Even if it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above
Applicant respectfully traverses the rationale to combine the references to support a rejection under Section 103. For example, Gillian does not relate to health and fitness. The terms "health" and "fitness" do not appear in Gillian. Thus, one skilled in the art would not be motivated to combine Gillian with the other references to arrive at Applicant's claimed invention. Even if, for the sake of argument, it was obvious to combine the references, they do not disclose or suggest all of the elements/features of the claims, as explained above.
6 Other dependent claims
Though the other dependent claims contain their own allowable subject matter, including amended claim 24, these claims should at least be allowable due to their dependence from allowable independent claims. Support for the amendment to claim 24 is found within Applicant's filed specification at page 8, line 37 to page 9, line 5, and page 9, lines 10-13. To expedite prosecution at this time, no further comment will be made.
Conclusion
The Applicant respectfully requests the Examiner enter this amendment and pass the claims to issue. The undersigned representative welcomes the opportunity to resolve any matters that may remain, formal or otherwise, via teleconference at the Examiner's discretion.
Respectfully submitted,
